Wherefore
WHAIR-for
adverb, conjunction
From the Saxon hwaer, where, and fore, for — literally “for which cause.” In the Authorized Version it renders the Hebrew lakhen and maddua, and the Greek dio, hothen, and dia touto: sometimes asking why, far more often declaring therefore.

Biblical Definition

Wherefore is the hinge-word of Scripture, and it works in two directions. Interrogatively it demands a reason: “Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread?” (Isa 55:2) — a question that indicts the whole trade of the natural man, who pays dearly for what cannot feed him. Far more frequently it is illative, drawing a conclusion out of what God has just said or done. This is its glory. The doctrine of Scripture is never left as bare information; it is fastened to the conscience by a wherefore. Because Christ humbled Himself unto death, “Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him” (Php 2:9) — the exaltation is not arbitrary, it is the Father’s answer to the obedience of the Son. Because our High Priest ever liveth, “Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost” (Heb 7:25): the security of the saints is deduced, not merely asserted. Because the engrafted word is able to save souls, “Wherefore lay apart all filthiness” (Jas 1:21). Mark the pattern — indicative first, imperative after; what God has done, then what the believer must do. The Authorized Version’s wherefore is the grammar of gospel logic, and to skip it is to sever duty from grace and leave a man with commands he has no power to keep.

Webster 1828 Definition

For which reason; for what reason; therefore. In Scripture chiefly the illative particle by which a duty is drawn out of a doctrine already declared.

expand to see more

WHEREFORE, adv. For which reason. Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them.

For what reason; why: as, wherefore did Sarah laugh? (Gen 18:13).

From where and fore; Saxon hwaer and fore.

In argument, the particle introducing the conclusion of a premise.

Scripturally, the joint at which the indicative of grace becomes the imperative of obedience (Jas 1:21).

Key Scripture

Isa 55:2 — "Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread? and your labour for that which satisfieth not? hearken diligently unto me, and eat ye that which is good, and let your soul delight itself in fatness."

Php 2:9 — "Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name:"

Heb 7:25 — "Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them."

Jas 1:21 — "Wherefore lay apart all filthiness and superfluity of naughtiness, and receive with meekness the engrafted word, which is able to save your souls."

Modern Corruption

Modern versions frequently dissolve the AV’s connective particles into sentence breaks, and modern preaching follows — doctrine is announced in one paragraph and duty demanded in another, with the logical joint between them quietly removed.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The loss here is not a redefinition but an amputation. When a translation or a sermon drops the connective, the hearer receives two disconnected things: a doctrine he is told to admire, and a command he is told to obey. He is never shown that the second grows out of the first. The result is the oldest error in practical religion — law without gospel, imperative without indicative — and it breeds either despair in the tender or self-righteousness in the hard. The Apostle never preaches that way. Romans spends eleven chapters on what God has done and opens the twelfth with I beseech you therefore. Ephesians spends three chapters on election, redemption, and adoption before the fourth says walk worthy. Strike the hinge and both halves fall.

Recover the plain sense: read every wherefore and therefore as an instruction to look backward before going forward. Ask what has just been said of God, of Christ, of the covenant — and then receive the duty as the fruit of it. This is not a grammatical nicety; it is the whole method by which the Spirit moves a doctrine from the understanding into the life. A believer who reads his Bible for its wherefores will never be able to separate believing from obeying, and will never be tempted to think obedience earns what grace has already given.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Saxon “for which”; in Scripture the illative particle fastening obedience to accomplished grace.

expand to see more

Wherefore — Saxon hwaer (where) + fore (for), “for which cause.”

Hebrew lakhen, therefore (Isa 55:2 uses the interrogative lammah).

Greek dio and dia touto, the standard illative particles of the Epistles (Php 2:9).

Interrogative sense: for what cause? (Gen 18:13; Exo 5:4).

Illative sense: the joint between doctrine and duty (Heb 7:25; Jas 1:21).

Usage

"Never read past a wherefore — it points back to the ground of the command that follows."

"Php 2:9 shows the word doing doctrinal work: exaltation follows humiliation by the Father’s reckoning."

"Isa 55:2 uses it to indict: the sinner’s spending is exposed by a single question."
